cards.explanation: The answer is False. The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), says “To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven…” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). He doesn't pick out a few favorite parts of life, friends. Even a batch of cookies has its time in the oven.

The answer is a time to be born and a time to die. Verse 2 says “…a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot…” (Ecclesiastes 3:2). The first day and the last day of a life sit side by side in one line. He could have started small, friends, but he went straight to the big stuff.

The answer is opposite. Born goes with die, plant goes with uproot, and break down goes with build (Ecclesiastes 3:2-3). Every time in the Teacher's list has its opposite waiting right beside it, friends. Pairs all the way down.

The answer is sad times and glad times. The verse says “…a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance…” (Ecclesiastes 3:4). Tears sit on one side and laughter on the other, and mourning sits right beside dancing. I think that's what makes this list feel so honest about life, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 5 says “…a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing…” (Ecclesiastes 3:5). So the Teacher names the hug and also the holding back, friends. Even this part of the list comes in a pair.

The answer is a time to discard. Verse 6 says “…a time to keep and a time to discard…” (Ecclesiastes 3:6). Keeping gets its season, and so does letting go. Anybody who has ever cleaned out a closet knows both of those times are real, friends.

The answer is speak. The verse says “…a time to be silent and a time to speak…” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Silence and speech both get their seasons, friends. I think the hard part is knowing which one the moment is asking for.

The answer is a time for peace. The last line of the Teacher's list says “…a time for war and a time for peace.” (Ecclesiastes 3:8). The list closes with the same kind of pair it has used the whole way through, friends. War gets matched with its opposite, peace.

The answer is beautiful. The Teacher says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Everything, friends, and in its time. After all those seasons of weeping and war, that's a gentle thing to hear.

The answer is False. The Teacher says God “…has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). So people can't take in all of it, from start to finish. It's a lot bigger than any of us, friends.

The answer is to rejoice and do good. The Teacher says, “I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live…” (Ecclesiastes 3:12). Two simple things, friends, and he says nothing is better. That's one I hope we all write down.

The answer is gift. Verse 13 says every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor, and then, “…this is the gift of God.” (Ecclesiastes 3:13). A gift is something handed to you, friends, not something you earn. And it includes the labor part.

The answer is that it endures forever. The Teacher says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Seasons come and go in his list, friends, but God's work lasts. It keeps going forever.

The answer is True. The verse says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Nothing taken, nothing added, friends. My own cookie dough could never promise that, since somebody always sneaks a scoop.

The answer is so that people would fear Him. Verse 14 ends, “God does it so that they should fear Him.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). The Teacher gives that as the reason, friends. It comes right after the part about God's work lasting forever.

The answer is True. The last line says, “…for God will call to account what has passed.” (Ecclesiastes 3:15). The Teacher just says it plain, friends, no extra frosting. Sometimes the short sentences are the ones that make you set your spatula down.
